title: Alexander More: free choice is intellect and will together, whether 'appetitive mind' or 'intellective appetite'
source_text: XLIII. Celeberrimus autem jam dictus Alexander Morus, cum Viris illis Doctis, censet intellectum atque voluntatem liberum arbitrium inter se veluti partiri: & liberum arbitrium non esse aliud quam intellectum atque voluntatem, quatenus hae duae facultates concurrunt, & quodam quasi vinculo, sive conjugio inter se continentur. In utra vero potius facultate consistat, in medio relinquit. Sicut enim, inquit, arbitrium intellectus terminatur in voluntate, ita libertas voluntatis radicem habet in intellectu. Adeo ut, ex ejus mente, liberum arbitrium dici possit intellectus quatenus voluntatem movet atque afficit: vel voluntas quatenus ab intellectu movetur. Sive ipsius Aristotelis verbis ἢ ὀρεκτικὸς νοῦς, ἢ ὄρεξις διανοητική. De Gratia & libero arbitrio disp. 1. thes. 21.
pass_a_gloss: But the already mentioned Most Celebrated Alexander More, with those Learned Men, thinks that intellect and will as it were share free choice between them: & that free choice is nothing else than intellect and will, inasmuch as these two faculties concur, & are held together among themselves by a certain as it were bond, or marriage. But in which faculty rather it consists, he leaves undecided. For as, he says, the choice of the intellect is terminated in the will, so the liberty of the will has its root in the intellect. So that, according to his mind, free choice can be called the intellect inasmuch as it moves and affects the will: or the will inasmuch as it is moved by the intellect. Or in the words of Aristotle himself either appetitive mind, or intellective appetite. On Grace & free choice disp. 1. thes. 21.
pass_b_english: Alexander More, the famous man already mentioned, holds with those learned men that intellect and will in a sense divide free choice between them. Free choice, he thinks, is nothing but intellect and will in so far as the two faculties work together and are held together by a kind of bond or marriage. Which of the two faculties it rests in more, he leaves open.

"For as the choice of the intellect ends in the will," he says, "so the freedom of the will has its root in the intellect." On his view, then, free choice can be called the intellect as it moves and affects the will, or the will as the intellect moves it. In Aristotle's own words, it is "either desiring mind or thinking desire" (On Grace and Free Choice, disputation 1, thesis 21).

choices.term: ἢ ὀρεκτικὸς νοῦς, ἢ ὄρεξις διανοητική
choices.english: either desiring mind or thinking desire
choices.why: Aristotle's formula for choice (Nicomachean Ethics VI.2) is rendered in plain words so that the chiasmus is visible.
